sources: Definitions checked against two independent written sources: Wikipedia, 'Fielding (cricket)' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fielding_(cricket) (naming system; 'silly' per the Oxford English Dictionary; slips numbered outwards from the wicket-keeper) and 'Glossary of cricket terms' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_cricket_terms (third man: behind the wicket-keeper on the off side, beyond slip and gully); and SportPlan, 'Cricket Fielding Positions Explained' https://www.sportplan.net/drills/Cricket/guides/cricket-fielding-positions-explained.jsp (same points; third man's purpose, also stated by https://www.cricketwriter.com/cricket-fielding-positions-third-man/).

Neither source, and no other we found, documents why the position is called 'third man'; the video says the origin is not documented. Field plans are illustrative, for a right-handed batter (mirrored for a left-hander); positions are neither fixed nor precisely defined and fielders can stand anywhere. short.vo: Third man. Silly mid-off. Deep backward square leg. Cricket's fielding names sound like nonsense. But they are a code, and once you can read it, you can read any field.
The first word gives the angle from the batter: leg, cover, mid-wicket, point.
A second word gives the distance. Short is closer. Deep or long is farther. And silly means so close that it looks dangerous, which is exactly where the name comes from.
Square means level with the batter, across the pitch. Backward and forward tilt the angle.
Close catchers have their own code. Slips are numbered outwards from the wicket-keeper: first slip, second slip, third slip. Together, the slip cordon.
Third man stands behind the wicket, on the off side, far beyond the slips. His job: stop the edges that fly past them and race to the boundary.
So why is it called third man? Honestly, nobody has a documented answer. The name is old, and the explanations you hear are only theories.
Now you can read any field. Follow for more Did You Know.

short.description:
Fielding positions explained: where is third man, and why are cricket's fielding names so strange? The names are a code: an angle word (leg, cover, mid-wicket, point) and a distance word (short, deep, long, silly). Slips are numbered outwards from the wicket-keeper; third man stands behind the wicket on the off side. Why is it called third man? No documented origin exists. Illustrative field plans for a right-handed batter. Sources: Wikipedia (Fielding (cricket); Glossary of cricket terms) and SportPlan's fielding positions guide.
